2027-05-09.title: The Ascension of the Lord
readings: As they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight
God mounts his throne to shouts of joy: a blare of trumpets for the Lord (or: Alleluia)
God seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places (or: Ephesians 4:1–13, shorter form 4:1–7, 11–13)
The Lord Jesus was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God
2027-05-09.alt: Solemnity, Year B. In India the Ascension is transferred from Thursday 6 May to this Sunday, and so the Seventh Sunday of Easter is not celebrated this year; where the Ascension was kept on Thursday, today is the Seventh Sunday of Easter (Acts 1:15–17, 20–26; 1 John 4:11–16; John 17:11b–19). Gloria and Creed; Preface of the Ascension; the proper form of the Communicantes in the Roman Canon. World Communications Day. The novena to the Holy Spirit continues until Pentecost. Regina Caeli at noon. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-05-09.verse: They said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up toward heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.”
theo: St Luke wrote two books, and today's first reading is the hinge between them. “In the first book, Theophilus, I wrote about all that Jesus did and taught from the beginning until the day when he was taken up to heaven.” The Gospel of Luke ends with the Ascension; the Acts of the Apostles begins with it. The Ascension is not an epilogue to the story of Jesus; it is the beginning of the story of the Church. Luke tells us that after his suffering Jesus “presented himself alive to them by many convincing proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God.” Forty is the number of preparation: the flood, Moses on the mountain, Israel in the desert, Elijah's journey, Jesus' fast. These forty days prepare the apostles for a new way of being with their Lord. And their last question shows how much they still have to learn: “Lord, is this the time when you will restore the kingdom to Israel?” Jesus does not scold them. He redirects them: “It is not for you to know the times or periods … But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.” That one verse is the table of contents of the whole Book of Acts.

Then the moment itself: “as they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight.” The cloud in the Bible is not weather; it is the sign of God's presence. The cloud led Israel through the desert, filled the tabernacle and the Temple, and overshadowed Jesus at the Transfiguration. Daniel saw “one like a human being coming with the clouds of heaven” to receive an everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:13–14). So Jesus does not go up into the sky as a rocket goes into space; he enters the glory of God, and he takes our human nature, his risen body with its wounds, with him. And immediately two men in white, like the two at the empty tomb, ask the disciples a question that is also for us: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up toward heaven?” The Ascension is not an invitation to stand and stare. The same Jesus “will come in the same way,” and until then there is work to do.

The Psalm is the song of a King's enthronement: “God has gone up with a shout, the Lord with the sound of a trumpet. Sing praises to God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises.” The Church has sung it on this feast from the earliest centuries. In the second reading Paul prays that the Ephesians may have “the eyes of your heart enlightened” to see what God has done: he “raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all rule and authority and power and dominion.” To sit at the right hand means to share the Father's power and glory. And Paul adds the astonishing consequence: God “has made him the head over all things for the church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.” The Head has gone into heaven, but the Body is still here, joined to him. Where the Head has gone, the Body is called to follow. (The alternative reading, Ephesians 4, makes the same point another way: “When he ascended on high … he gave gifts to his people,” apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers, to build up the Body.)

Mark's Gospel, in its closing verses, gives the Ascension in a few strong lines. Jesus sends the eleven: “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.” Belief and baptism will bring salvation; signs will accompany those who believe. Then: “the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God.” And at once, without a pause: “And they went out and proclaimed the good news everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by the signs that accompanied it.” That is the key to the whole feast. Jesus sits at the right hand of God, and at the same moment he works with his disciples on earth. He is not further away; he is closer, no longer limited to one place, present to every place where the Gospel is proclaimed. These verses (Mark 16:9–20) are missing from some ancient manuscripts, but the Church received them as inspired Scripture, and Trent confirmed the canon with them.

Today is also World Communications Day, kept on the Sunday before Pentecost since 1967, at the wish of the Second Vatican Council. It is fitting. The Lord who ascends gives his Church a message for “the whole creation” and the ends of the earth. In our age the ends of the earth are reached by phone screens and radio, by newspapers and the internet. Every Christian with a mobile phone is in some way an evangelist, for good or ill. And between the Ascension and Pentecost, the Church does what the apostles did: they returned to Jerusalem and devoted themselves to prayer “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). We are in those nine days. Let us look up to where Christ has gone, and then look around at the world he sends us to, and pray with his Mother: Come, Holy Spirit.
conn: Theophilus.
The name means “friend of God.” Luke dedicates both his books to him (Luke 1:3; Acts 1:1); he may have been a patron, or the name may stand for every reader who loves God.
Forty days.
Only Luke gives the number. It echoes Moses on Sinai (Exodus 24:18), Elijah's journey to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8) and Jesus' fast in the desert (Luke 4:2): a time of preparation before a new beginning.
The place.
Luke places the Ascension near Bethany (Luke 24:50), on the Mount of Olives (Acts 1:12), the mountain from which, according to Zechariah 14:4, the Lord would come in the last days.
The cloud.

The sign of God's glorious presence: the pillar of cloud (Exodus 13:21), the cloud on the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34), the cloud of the Transfiguration (Mark 9:7), and the clouds of the Son of Man (Daniel 7:13).
Two men in white.
They recall the two men in dazzling clothes at the empty tomb (Luke 24:4) and Moses and Elijah at the Transfiguration (Luke 9:30). Their question turns the apostles from gazing to witnessing.
“Restore the kingdom to Israel.”
The hope of Israel's renewal was real and good (Luke 1:32–33; 24:21). Jesus does not deny it, but reveals a wider kingdom, reaching the ends of the earth through the Spirit.
The right hand of God.

A royal image from Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse most quoted in the New. To sit at the right hand is to share the King's authority. The Creed says: “he ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father.”
The ending of Mark.

Mark 16:9–20, the “longer ending,” is absent from the oldest Greek manuscripts but was widely known from the second century (St Irenaeus quotes it). The Church accepts it as part of the inspired, canonical Scripture.
Psalm 47.
An enthronement psalm. Verse 5, “God has gone up with a shout,” has been sung on the Ascension since ancient times, and often gives the feast's Alleluia verse.
World Communications Day.

Called for by the Second Vatican Council's decree Inter Mirifica (1963) and first kept in 1967; it is a worldwide day asked for by the Council itself. The Pope's message is usually published on 24 January, the feast of St Francis de Sales, patron of writers and journalists.
In India.

The Latin bishops of India keep the Ascension on the Sunday after the fortieth day, so that the whole people of God can take part, as they do with the Epiphany and Corpus Christi (please verify with your diocesan Ordo).
altar: The Preface of the Ascension prays that Christ ascended “not to distance himself from our lowly state but that we, his members, might be confident of following where he, our Head and Founder, has gone before.” Every Mass is a door opened between earth and heaven, where the ascended Lord comes down to us under the signs of bread and wine.

The Letter to the Hebrews says that Christ “entered into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf” (Hebrews 9:24). The sacrifice of Calvary, offered once for all, is presented by our High Priest for ever before the Father, and the same sacrifice is made present on our altars.

St Leo the Great taught (in substance) that what was visible in our Redeemer has passed over into the sacraments. The disciples could no longer touch him; we can receive him. The ascended Lord is not absent: in the Eucharist he is truly, really and substantially present, Body and Blood, soul and divinity.
outline: Picture a crowd at an airport watching a plane disappear into the clouds. Ask: what do people do after the plane is gone?
Point 1 · Why do you stand looking up?
Point 2 · Seated at the right hand
Our human nature in the glory of God.
Point 3 · Head over all things for the church
The Head in heaven, the Body on earth.
Point 4 · Go into all the world
The Lord who works with us.
The apostles walking down the Mount of Olives back to the city, and Mary waiting for them in the upper room.
live: Each morning this week pray Colossians 3:1: seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Then decide one thing you will do today for heaven's sake.
Choose one concrete act of witness: invite someone to Mass, speak of your faith at work, or visit a sick person in the parish.
Use your phone as a disciple
On World Communications Day, review what you post and forward. Share one message of hope or one Gospel verse, and refuse to forward one rumour or harsh word.
Continue the novena to the Holy Spirit with your family until Pentecost, perhaps with a decade of the Rosary each evening, as the apostles prayed with Mary.
fathers: St Augustine (Sermon on the Ascension, in substance)

Today our Lord Jesus Christ ascended into heaven; let our hearts ascend with him. He is there, yet he is with us here; we are here, yet we are with him there. He is in heaven, and still he says to the persecutor: why do you persecute me? because he is the Head and we are his Body.

The Ascension of Christ is our own elevation; where the glory of the Head has gone before, the hope of the body is also called. Today we are not only confirmed as possessors of paradise, but in Christ we have entered the heights of heaven.
What was visible in our Redeemer has passed over into the sacraments; and faith, made more excellent and firmer, now follows the teaching of the Spirit and not bodily sight.
St Gregory the Great (Homily on Mark 16, in substance)

The signs at the beginning were needed for the faith to grow, as we water a young plant until it takes root. Now the Church does spiritually what the apostles did bodily: she casts out the demon of sin, speaks the new language of praise, and lays hands of kindness on the sick.

Today our nature, which once was thought unworthy of the earth, has been lifted above the heavens and seated on the royal throne. The angels who once guarded paradise against us now see our nature at the right hand of God.
magis: Christ's body was glorified at the moment of his Resurrection; the Ascension marks the definitive entrance of Jesus' humanity into God's heavenly domain.

Only the one who came from the Father can return to him: Christ opens the way for us, and as High Priest he intercedes constantly for us as the mediator who assures us of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit.
Being seated at the Father's right hand signifies the inauguration of the Messiah's kingdom, the fulfilment of Daniel's vision: a kingdom that will have no end.
The missionary mandate: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations.” Sent by God to the nations, the Church strives to preach the Gospel to all.
United with Christ by Baptism, believers already truly share in the heavenly life of the risen Christ, though this life remains hidden with Christ in God.
An annual day should be held in every diocese to teach the faithful their duties in the use of the means of social communication, to pray for this cause and to support the Church's work in it.
The information provided by the media is at the service of the common good; society has a right to information based on truth, freedom, justice and solidarity.
Every baptized person is a missionary disciple; we no longer say that we are disciples and missionaries, but that we are always missionary disciples.
saints: Seventh Sunday of Easter (not kept in India this year)

Where the Ascension is kept on Thursday, today the Church reads of the choice of Matthias and of Jesus' prayer for his disciples, “Holy Father, protect them in your name.” In India these readings are not used this year; the feast of St Matthias comes on Friday 14 May.

10 May: St John of Avila (optional). 12 May: Sts Nereus and Achilleus; St Pancras (optional). 13 May: Our Lady of Fatima (optional). 14 May: ST MATTHIAS, APOSTLE (feast). 15 May: last weekday of Easter; Vigil of Pentecost in the evening. 16 May: PENTECOST SUNDAY.
2027-05-09.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, King of glory, today you ascended above all the heavens and took your seat at the right hand of the Father. You did not leave us orphans: you took our human nature into the glory of God, and you remain with us, working with your Church and confirming her word. Lift up our hearts to where you are, so that we seek the things that are above; and send us down the mountain into the world, to proclaim the good news to the whole creation. Be the Head of your Body, the Church; give us the eyes of the heart to see the hope to which you have called us; and make all who speak and write and broadcast in our time servants of truth and peace. With Mary your Mother and the apostles we wait for the Holy Spirit whom you promised. Come again in glory, Lord Jesus, as you went into heaven. You live and reign with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Alleluia. Amen.

quick: Forty days after the Resurrection, Jesus promised the Holy Spirit and sent the apostles to be his witnesses to the ends of the earth; then a cloud took him from their sight.
God seated Christ at his right hand, above every power, and made him head of the Church, his body.
The disciples went out and proclaimed the Gospel everywhere, while the Lord worked with them.
2027-05-09.action: Share one Gospel verse or message of hope with someone today, in person or on your phone, as an act of witness on World Communications Day.
2027-05-09.question: Am I standing and looking up, or am I going out as the Lord's witness?
catechism: Christ our High Priest intercedes for us.
kidsaint: Carlo was an Italian teenager who loved video games, football and computers. He also loved Jesus in the Eucharist and went to Mass every day. He used his computer skills to make a website about Eucharistic miracles that people still visit today. He died of leukaemia in 2006 at fifteen and was declared a saint in 2025. He said: the Eucharist is my highway to heaven. Lesson: you can use your phone and computer to share Jesus with the world.
2027-05-09.special: Solemnity of the Ascension (India). Gloria and Creed; Preface of the Ascension; World Communications Day; Seventh Sunday of Easter not celebrated this year in India. Regina Caeli at noon.
term: Seated at the right hand of the Father

A phrase of the Creed from Psalm 110:1. It does not mean a place in the sky but that the risen Christ, in his glorified humanity, shares the glory, power and kingship of the Father, and intercedes for us there.

family.explain: Forty days after Easter Jesus took his friends to a hill, blessed them, and went up to heaven. A cloud hid him. Two angels said: why are you looking up at the sky? Jesus will come back! Now go and tell everyone about him. Jesus is with the Father, and he is also with us every day. Today is also Mother's Day in many places: we thank God for our mothers, and for Mary, the Mother of Jesus, who prayed with the apostles while they waited for the Holy Spirit.
family.intention: We pray for missionaries all over the world, for all who work in newspapers, television and the internet, and for our mothers.
family.ask: Ask: “Who can we tell about Jesus this week?” Choose one person and pray for them together every night until Pentecost.

illus: When a fisherman from Poovar took a job in the Gulf, his small daughter cried at the airport as the plane disappeared into the clouds. For a long time she would not eat. Her mother told her: Appa has not gone away from us; he has gone ahead for us. Every month money came home, and every evening a video call. Two years later the family moved into a small concrete house built with his wages. On the day it was blessed, the girl, now eight, said to the parish priest: Appa went away so he could prepare a place for us. The priest said: that is exactly what Jesus said on the day he went into the clouds.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, King of glory, lift up our hearts to you, and send us out as your witnesses. Come, Holy Spirit. Alleluia. Amen.
share: Why do you stand looking up toward heaven? (Acts 1:11). Is my faith more gazing than going? Where is the Lord sending me?
He has made him the head over all things for the church, which is his body (Ephesians 1:22–23). How do I live as a member of Christ's Body in my parish?
The Lord worked with them and confirmed the message (Mark 16:20). When have I felt the Lord working with me?
pm.resp: God mounts his throne to shouts of joy: a blare of trumpets for the Lord.
interc: For the Church spread through the world, that she may witness to the risen and ascended Lord to the ends of the earth.
For all who work in the media and on the internet, that they may serve truth, peace and human dignity, and for Christians to use their phones and screens for good.
For missionaries, especially those working in difficult places, that the Lord may work with them.
For our mothers, living and dead, and for all mothers who are anxious for their children.
For our group, that we may pray with Mary in these days and receive the Holy Spirit at Pentecost.
pm.close: Almighty Father, your Son ascended to your right hand, our Head gone before us. Keep our hearts fixed on him, and send us his Spirit, so that we may be his witnesses everywhere. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, have you ever stood at an airport and watched a plane carry away someone you love? You stand at the glass and watch until it is only a dot, and then it disappears into the clouds. You keep looking a little longer. Then someone touches your shoulder: come, let us go home.

That is what happened to the apostles on the Mount of Olives. Jesus blessed them, and as they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight (Acts 1:9). They kept staring. And two men in white touched their shoulders, so to speak: Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up toward heaven? (Acts 1:11).

First, the Ascension tells us where Jesus has gone. Not to some planet far away. The cloud in the Bible is the sign of God's glory. Jesus has entered the glory of God, and he has taken our human nature with him: his risen body, with his wounds, now sits at the right hand of the Father (Ephesians 1:20). A man like us is in the heart of God. That is our future too. Where the Head has gone, the Body will follow.

Second, the Ascension tells us that Jesus has not left us. St Paul says God made him the head over all things for the church, which is his body (Ephesians 1:22–23). The Head is in heaven; the Body is here. You are that Body. And Mark tells us something wonderful: they went out and proclaimed the good news everywhere, while the Lord worked with them (Mark 16:20). He sits at the right hand of God and at the same time works with us. He is not further away; he is nearer, because he is no longer in one place but with every disciple everywhere.

Third, the Ascension gives us a job. Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation (Mark 16:15). You will be my witnesses to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8). The angels did not let the apostles stand and stare. Our faith is not only looking up; it is also going out.

Today is World Communications Day. Two thousand years ago the apostles walked on dusty roads. Today the ends of the earth are in your pocket, on your phone. What do you send and forward? Rumours, gossip, anger? Or hope, truth, and the Good News? Every Christian with a phone can be a witness, like St Carlo Acutis, the teenager who used the internet to spread love for the Eucharist.

Finally, the apostles did not rush out at once. Jesus told them to wait for the Holy Spirit. So they went back to Jerusalem and prayed, together with Mary the mother of Jesus (Acts 1:14). We are in those days now. In this Mass the ascended Lord comes down to us in his Body and Blood. Let us receive him, lift up our hearts to where he is, and with Mary pray every day this week: Come, Holy Spirit. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, forty days after Easter, Jesus went up to heaven. A cloud hid him. His friends kept looking up at the sky, and two angels said: why are you looking up? Jesus will come back! Now go and tell everybody about him.
Jesus is in heaven with the Father, and he is also with us every day, especially in Holy Communion. Let us look up and say: Jesus, I love you; and then go and be kind to someone!

opts.a: A life worthy of the calling
intro: In the alternative second reading Paul draws a practical lesson from the Ascension: the risen Lord has gone up and given gifts, so we must live in unity and build up his body.

points.apply: Practise patience with one difficult person this week.

sub: One Lord, one faith, one baptism.
One God and Father of all.
points.apply: Pray for unity in your family, parish and the whole Church.

sub: The psalm of the ascending King.
points.apply: Offer your parish one gift of your time or talent.

concl: The ascended Lord pours out gifts so that his body on earth may grow in unity.
We honour his Ascension by living worthy of our calling.
opts.resolve: This week I will practise patience, pray for unity, and offer my parish one gift.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, the Ascension can seem far from daily life. Jesus goes up; we stay here. But St Paul draws a very practical lesson from it. Writing from prison, he says: I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to lead a life worthy of the calling to which you have been called (Ephesians 4:1).

What does such a life look like? With all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, making every effort to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Ephesians 4:2–3). The prophet Micah had said the same: to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God (Micah 6:8). The ascended Lord is not honoured by staring at the sky but by patience in the kitchen, in the office and in the parish committee.

Paul continues: there is one body and one Spirit… one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all (Ephesians 4:4–6). Israel prayed every day: hear, O Israel, the LORD is our God, the LORD alone (Deuteronomy 6:4). Because God is one, his people must be one. Every quarrel in the Church wounds the body whose Head has ascended into heaven.

Then Paul quotes a psalm about a king going up in triumph: when he ascended on high he made captivity itself a captive; he gave gifts to his people (Ephesians 4:8; Psalm 68:18). The ascended Christ does not leave us empty-handed. The gifts he gave were that some would be apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, some pastors and teachers, to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ (Ephesians 4:11–12). Every Christian has received a gift for others.

So let us celebrate the Ascension by living worthy of our calling. Be patient with one difficult person. Pray and work for unity. Offer your parish one gift: teaching catechism, singing in the choir, visiting the sick, cleaning the church. And at this Mass, receive the ascended Lord who gives himself as the greatest gift of all. Alleluia. Amen.

intro: Paul prays that the eyes of our hearts may be enlightened to see the hope to which God has called us. The Ascension shows us that hope: Christ in glory, praying for us, and coming again.

points.apply: Ask the Holy Spirit each morning this week: open the eyes of my heart.

points.h: He lives to intercede for us
points.apply: Pray through Christ for someone in great need.

points.h: He will come in the same way
points.apply: Put right one thing you would not want him to find undone.

concl: The ascended Christ is our hope: he is in glory, he prays for us, and he will return.
With enlightened hearts we live in that hope.
opts.resolve: This week I will pray each morning for enlightened eyes and live ready for the Lord's return.
homily: Dear friends, in today's second reading St Paul prays a beautiful prayer for us. He asks that God may give us a spirit of wisdom and revelation, so that, with the eyes of your heart enlightened, you may know what is the hope to which he has called you (Ephesians 1:17–18). The Ascension is about hope, and hope needs eyes of the heart to see it.

Our physical eyes saw the cloud take Jesus away. The eyes of the heart see more. They see that the man Jesus, with his wounded and risen body, now sits at the right hand of the Father. The psalm had foretold it: the LORD says to my lord, sit at my right hand (Psalm 110:1). The psalmist prayed: open my eyes, so that I may behold wondrous things (Psalm 119:18). Let us ask for those eyes today.

What is Jesus doing at the right hand of the Father? The Letter to the Hebrews answers: he is able for all time to save those who approach God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them (Hebrews 7:25). At this very moment Jesus is praying for you. He shows the Father his wounds and presents your name. When we pray through Christ our Lord, as the Church does at the end of her prayers, we join a prayer that is already rising in heaven.

And the angels promised the apostles: this Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven (Acts 1:11). Daniel had seen one like a human being coming with the clouds of heaven (Daniel 7:13). Christ will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead. We do not know the day. So the hope of the Ascension is also a call to be ready.

So let us lift the eyes of our hearts. Let us remember that Jesus prays for us. Let us live each day so that we would be glad to see him come. And at this Mass, where the ascended Lord comes to us hidden in bread, let us receive a foretaste of the glory to which he has called us. Alleluia. Amen.

intro: The Ascension as the beginning of the Church's mission: a question from heaven, a King enthroned, a Head joined to his Body, and a Lord who works with his witnesses.

points.h: Why do you stand looking up?
q: As they continued walking and talking, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated the two of them, and Elijah ascended in a whirlwind into heaven.
They said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up toward heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.”
points.apply: This week, after each time of prayer, ask: Lord, where are you sending me today? and do one thing in answer.

sub: Our nature in the glory of God.
q: The Lord says to my lord, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool.”
God put this power to work in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places,
points.apply: Pray slowly each night this week the line of the Creed: he ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father, and thank him for interceding for you.

points.h: Head over all things for the church
sub: The eyes of the heart enlightened.
The Head in heaven, the Body on earth.
Where the Head has gone, the Body follows.
q: To him was given dominion and glory and kingship, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that shall not pass away, and his kingship is one that shall never be destroyed.
And he has put all things under his feet and has made him the head over all things for the church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.
points.apply: Take one practical step to serve your parish, the Body of Christ, this week: a ministry, a visit, a contribution of time.

sub: The ends of the earth in our pockets.
The Lord who works with us.
q: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger who announces peace, who brings good news, who announces salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns.”
And he said to them, “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.
points.apply: On this World Communications Day, share one message of hope or a Gospel verse, and decide not to forward anything untrue or unkind.

concl: The Ascension is not Jesus going away but Jesus going ahead: our human nature is seated in the glory of God, and the Head draws the Body after him.
Seated at the right hand of the Father, the Lord works with his witnesses everywhere; with Mary we wait for the Spirit, and then we go into all the world.
2027-05-09.resolve: Lift up your heart each morning this week, and go out each day to bear one witness to the risen and ascended Lord.
